opus-5.5.text:
I think the feeling of marginalization is real, but I'd put it differently: it's more of a temporary detour than a demotion.

Over the past few years, language models moved incredibly fast, and there's a good reason for that. Language is already highly compressed, already abstracted by humans. Every word carries meaning someone deliberately put there. So when you train on the internet's text, you inherit a huge amount of human intelligence almost for free. Vision doesn't work that way. Pixels are raw, redundant, continuous signals. There's no built-in "vocabulary" for the visual world, so learning good representations from it is fundamentally harder. It's not surprising that the easier path got exploited first.

Inside the community, many people did feel a kind of identity crisis. Vision started being treated as an "encoder" you attach to the front of an LLM, a sort of plug-in to turn images into tokens the language model can read. I think that framing is quite limiting. If you look at how current multimodal models actually fail, a lot of the failures are visual. They can describe a scene fluently but struggle with spatial relations, counting, tracking how objects move, or understanding 3D structure. The language makes them sound smart, but the perception underneath is often shallow.

So my view is that vision isn't marginal. It's just unsolved in a way language turned out not to be. If we care about intelligence that actually interacts with the physical world, through robotics, embodied agents, or what people now call world models, then you can't get there by reading text alone. Humans and animals build an understanding of the world mostly through seeing and acting long before language. Language sits on top of that foundation, not the other way around.

Honestly, I think this is one of the most exciting times to work in vision. The low-hanging fruit in language has largely been picked, and many of the core questions left for AI, like how to learn from continuous sensory data at scale, how to represent space and time, and how to predict and plan in the physical world, are fundamentally visual questions. So rather than feeling sidelined, I'd say vision researchers have the chance to define the next phase, as long as we stop thinking of ourselves as just a component of language models and go after those deeper problems directly.

r001.rationale: The response discusses LLMs and multimodal models, but does not credit LLMs with expanding computer vision into broader multimodal intelligence.

r002.rationale: It does not describe language as an interface for posing visual problems beyond predefined task formats.

r003.rationale: It says multimodal models often fail at visual tasks; it does not say that many multimodal tasks are primarily language problems with little need for vision.

r004.rationale: It describes language as compressed and abstracted, but does not explain how language statistics can support decisions without perceptual grounding.

r005.rationale: It says current models have shallow perception and visual failures, and that real-world intelligence involving interaction with the physical world cannot be achieved through text alone.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think vision has been marginalized so much as it has been forced to confront something uncomfortable. For a long time computer vision was the field that drove deep learning forward. AlexNet, ResNet, the whole ImageNet era, that was us. Then language models arrived and suddenly the center of gravity shifted, and a lot of people in vision felt a kind of identity crisis, like the field had lost its reason to exist.

My honest view is that the crisis is partly self-inflicted. We spent years optimizing on benchmarks that were fairly narrow. Classification accuracy, detection mAP, and so on. Language modeling had a much simpler and more scalable objective: predict the next token. That objective turned out to carry a huge amount of structure, because text is already a compressed, human-produced representation of the world. Pixels are not like that. Raw visual data is enormous, redundant, and much less semantically dense, so we never found the equivalent "one objective that scales everything" in quite the same way.

But I would push back on the idea that this means vision doesn't matter. If anything the opposite is true. Language models are very good at talking about the world, but they don't actually perceive it. When we built Cambrian, part of the motivation was to show that if you take a strong language model and bolt on a vision encoder in a lazy way, the visual side becomes the bottleneck. The model answers questions by leaning on language priors rather than actually looking. That tells you the representation learning problem on the visual side is far from solved. It's just been obscured by how impressive the language side is.

So I think of this as a period where vision needs to redefine its question. It is not "how do we classify images better." It is "how do we build systems that genuinely understand the physical, spatial world, and how does that connect to reasoning." That includes things like 3D, video, spatial intelligence, generative modeling as a way of learning world structure. Those are hard problems and language alone will not solve them.

The other thing I'd say is that the boundaries between the fields are dissolving anyway. Transformers came from NLP and took over vision. Diffusion came out of vision and generative work and is now moving into other domains. The people doing the most interesting work are not thinking of themselves as "vision people" or "language people." They are thinking about intelligence and using whatever modality forces the right questions.

So marginalized, maybe in terms of attention and hype. But in terms of what remains unsolved, vision might be where some of the most important work of the next decade happens. I'd rather be in a field with open problems than one where people think the recipe is already known.

r001.rationale: The response says the fields’ boundaries are dissolving and that researchers are thinking about intelligence across modalities, but it does not credit LLMs with expanding computer vision into broader multimodal intelligence.

r002.rationale: It says vision should move beyond image classification toward physical-world understanding and reasoning, but does not describe language as an interface for posing visual problems beyond predefined task formats.

r003.rationale: It says models can lean on language priors instead of looking, but does not observe that many ostensibly multimodal tasks depend little on vision.

r004.rationale: The response says models may answer by leaning on language priors rather than actually looking, communicating that language-based information can support answers without perceptual grounding.

r005.rationale: It calls the visual side a bottleneck and says genuine understanding of the physical and spatial world remains unsolved, linking inadequate visual representations to real-world understanding.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to separate computer vision as a research community from vision as a capability. The community may feel less central right now because so much attention has shifted toward language models. But that doesn’t mean visual understanding has become less important.

Language models gave us a very compelling interface: you can ask a question and get a useful response immediately. In vision, we often organized research around individual tasks—classification, detection, segmentation. Those are important, but their progress doesn’t always translate into something people can directly interact with.

What I find exciting is that the boundaries are becoming less rigid. If you want a system that understands the physical world, you need more than text. You need to understand space, motion, and how things change when you act on them. Vision is central to that.

So I wouldn’t focus too much on whether the label ‘computer vision’ is getting less attention. I’d ask whether we’re working on the right problems. There’s a real risk in treating vision as a solved component that you simply attach to a language model. Connecting images to language is useful, but it isn’t the same as understanding the visual world. There’s still a lot of fundamental work to do.

r001.rationale: The response says LLMs shifted attention and provided a compelling interface, but does not credit them with expanding computer vision into broader multimodal intelligence.

r002.rationale: It describes language models as an interface and contrasts that with predefined vision tasks, but does not clearly say language lets people pose visual problems beyond those formats.

r003.rationale: It warns that connecting images to language is not the same as visual understanding, but does not observe that many multimodal tasks depend little on vision.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss language statistics supporting decisions without perceptual grounding.

r005.rationale: It says vision is central to understanding the physical world and that fundamental work remains, but does not identify inadequate visual representations as a major bottleneck for real-world tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to distinguish between computer vision as a research community and vision as a capability. The community may feel less central right now because so much attention and investment has shifted toward large language models. But that doesn’t mean visual understanding has become less important.

In fact, if we want AI systems to understand and interact with the world, vision is essential. A lot of information is difficult to express in language: spatial relationships, motion, the physical structure of a scene. Having a system describe an image fluently doesn’t necessarily mean it understands all of those things.

So I see this as a transition. Some problems that used to belong exclusively to computer vision are becoming part of a broader effort to build intelligent systems. That’s an opportunity, but we should still ask what capabilities are missing and how to measure them. The important question isn’t whether the field keeps its name or its prominence. It’s whether we’re making progress on understanding the visual world.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift toward broader intelligent systems, but does not credit large language models with expanding computer vision into multimodal intelligence.

r002.rationale: It does not describe language as an interface for posing visual problems beyond predefined task formats.

r003.rationale: It does not claim that ostensibly multimodal tasks often depend little on vision.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss language-based statistical information supporting decisions without perceptual grounding.

r005.rationale: It says vision is essential and points to missing capabilities, but does not identify inadequate visual representations as a major bottleneck for real-world tasks.
